title: Various events from the same counsel
paragraphs: Jacques Amyot, grand almoner of France, one day told me a story that does great honour to one of our princes — and ours he was on several very good counts, though originally of foreign extraction. During our first commotions, at the siege of Rouen, this prince was warned by the queen-mother of a conspiracy against his life, with her letters naming the very man who was to carry it out: a gentleman of Anjou or Maine who normally frequented the prince's household. The prince did not breathe a syllable of this to anyone. The next day he went up to St Catherine's Mount, from which our battery was playing against the town (for the siege was still on), accompanied by the said lord almoner and another bishop. He saw the gentleman who had been pointed out to him, and sent for him at once. When the man came before him, already pale and trembling under the weight of his guilt, the prince said: "Monsieur So-and-so, you can guess what I have to say to you; your face gives it away. There's no point in disguising your scheme — I'm so well informed of your business that any attempt to conceal or deny it will only make things worse for you. You know perfectly well such-and-such details" (the most secret circumstances of the conspiracy), "so as you value your life, confess the whole truth of the plot." The poor man, seeing himself trapped and convicted (the whole business had been disclosed to the queen by one of the accomplices), didn't know what to do. He folded his hands, begged and pleaded for mercy, and threw himself at his prince's feet. The prince raised him up and went on: "Now, sir, tell me — have I ever offended you? Have I, out of private hatred or malice, wronged any kinsman or friend of yours? It's not even three weeks since I first laid eyes on you. What could possibly have driven you to attempt my death?" In a trembling voice the gentleman replied that it was no private grudge against him personally, but the general interest of his party; that certain people had urged him on, persuading him it would be a meritorious act, by any means available, to wipe out so great and so powerful an enemy of their religion. "Well," said the prince, "I'll show you how much more charitable my religion is than yours. Yours has counselled you to kill me, without hearing me speak, without my having given you any cause for offence; mine commands me to forgive you, even though by your own confession you stand convicted of a design to kill me without reason. Get out. Don't let me see you again. And if you're wise, choose more honest counsellors from now on for your schemes."

The Emperor Augustus, while in Gaul, received reliable information of a conspiracy that L. Cinna was contriving against him. He resolved to make an example of the man, and to that end summoned his friends to meet in council the next morning. But the intervening night he spent in great inner agitation, considering that he was about to put to death a young man from an illustrious family, nephew to the great Pompey. The thought drove him into a series of passionate outbursts. "What then," he said, "am I to live in perpetual anxiety and alarm, and let my would-be assassin wander freely about? Will he go unpunished for having conspired against my life — a life I've defended through so many civil wars, so many battles by land and sea? After settling universal peace over the whole world, am I to pardon a man who's plotted not just to murder me but to slaughter me at sacrifice?" — for the plan was to kill him while he officiated. After a long silence he started up again, louder, raging at himself: "Why are you alive, if so many would benefit from your death? Will there be no end to your reprisals and cruelties? Is your life worth so much that so much harm must be done to preserve it?" His wife Livia, seeing him in this perplexity, said: "Will you take a woman's advice? Do as the physicians do — when the usual remedies fail, try the opposite. Severity has got you nowhere so far: Lepidus followed Salvidienus, Murena followed Lepidus, Caepio followed Murena, Egnatius followed Caepio. Try sweetness and clemency now. Cinna is convicted; pardon him. He'll never have the heart to harm you afterwards, and it'll add to your glory." Augustus was relieved to find an advocate of his own inclination. He thanked his wife, countermanded the summons to council, and ordered Cinna to be brought to him alone. When Cinna arrived, the room cleared and a chair set for him, Augustus said: "First, Cinna, I ask you to hear me out patiently. Don't interrupt — I'll give you time to answer afterwards. You know, Cinna, that I took you prisoner in the enemy's camp, where you were not merely an enemy by circumstance but an enemy by birth. I spared your life, restored all your goods, and finally set you up so comfortably by my generosity that the victors envied the defeated. The priestly office you petitioned me for, I granted you — after denying it to others whose fathers had always borne arms in my service. After all these favours, you've undertaken to kill me." Cinna cried out that he was very far from harbouring any such wicked thought. "You're not keeping your promise, Cinna," Augustus continued, "that you wouldn't interrupt me. Yes, you've undertaken to murder me, in such a place, on such a day, in such company, in such a manner." At those words, seeing Cinna struck dumb — not because of his promise but because his conscience had collapsed under the weight of the evidence — Augustus went on: "Now, to what end were you going to do it? To be emperor? Believe me, the Republic is in a sorry state if I'm the only man standing between you and the empire. You can't even defend your own household — only the other day you were beaten in a lawsuit by a mere freed slave's interest. Have you no means, no power anywhere except enough to take on Caesar? I'll step down from the throne if I'm the only obstacle to your hopes. Do you think the Paulli, the Fabii, the Cossii, the Servilii, and so many other noble Romans — noble not just in name but by the virtue that honours their nobility — would tolerate you?" After this, and a great deal more (he spoke for two long hours), he ended: "Now go, Cinna. Go. I give you the life I'd already given you once, when you were an enemy — and now I give it back to you again, traitor and parricide as you are. Let friendship begin between us from this moment, and let's see whether I have given, or you have received, your life with the better faith." And with that he left him. Some time later he advanced Cinna to the consulship, complaining that Cinna hadn't had the nerve to ask for it. He kept him afterwards as a very close friend, and was eventually made sole heir to his entire estate. Now — from the time of this episode, which befell Augustus in the fortieth year of his life, he never had another conspiracy or attempt made against him. He reaped the proper reward of his generous clemency. But things didn't go that way with our prince. His moderation and mercy did not protect him; he later fell into the net of a similar treason. So vain and futile a thing is human prudence; through all our projects, counsels, and precautions, Fortune will still be mistress of events.

We call physicians fortunate when they hit upon a lucky cure — as if theirs were the only art that couldn't stand on its own legs, whose foundations were too weak to support themselves, and as if no other art needed Fortune's hand to help it. For my part I think of medicine as much good or ill as anyone could want me to, since, thank God, we have no traffic with each other. I'm of the opposite humour to other men: I generally despise it; but when I'm sick, instead of recanting and coming to terms with it, I start to hate and fear it even more. I tell those who urge me to take medicine that they must at least give me time to recover my strength and health so I can better withstand the violence and danger of their potions. I let nature work, supposing her sufficiently armed with teeth and claws to defend herself against the assaults of illness and to uphold that structure whose dissolution she dreads. My fear is that, instead of helping her where she's grappling with disease, I'd be assisting her opponent and only piling more work on her.
Now, I say that not only in medicine but in other more reliable arts, Fortune has a very great share.

The poetic raptures, the flights of fancy that ravish and carry the author out of himself — why shouldn't we attribute them to his good fortune, since he himself admits they exceed his own capacity and force, acknowledging that they come from something other than himself, and that he has them no more in his power than orators say they have those extraordinary surges that sometimes push them beyond their own design? It's the same in painting, where strokes will sometimes slip from the painter's hand so far beyond his intention and his skill that they astonish even him. But Fortune shows her share in such things even more plainly through the graces and elegances we find in them — beyond, sometimes even without, the workman's awareness. A competent reader often discovers in another's writing perfections the author himself never intended or noticed, a richer sense and a more striking turn of phrase.

As for military enterprises, anyone can see how great a hand Fortune has in them. Even in our deliberations and counsels there must surely be something of chance and good luck mixed in with human prudence; for what wisdom can do on its own is no great matter. The keener, quicker, and more apprehensive it is, the more weakness it discovers in itself, and the more apt it is to distrust itself. I'm of Sulla's opinion; and when I look closely at the most glorious feats of war, it seems to me that those who conduct them use counsel and debate only for form's sake, leaving the best part of the enterprise to Fortune, and, leaning on her, breaking at every turn the bounds of military doctrine and the rules of war. There happen sometimes, in their deliberations, fortuitous bursts of energy and strange furies that mostly drive them to follow the worst-grounded plans, and swell their courage beyond reason's limits. That's why several of the great captains of old, to justify these rash resolutions, were obliged to tell their soldiers that some inspiration, some sign or omen, had invited them to the attempt.

So, in this doubt and uncertainty — in the short-sightedness of human wisdom that struggles to see and choose what's best because of the difficulties carried in by the various circumstances of things — the surest way, in my view, even without any other consideration urging us to it, is to pitch upon whatever has the greatest appearance of honesty and justice. If we can't be certain of the shortest road, let's keep to the straightest and most direct one. In the two examples I just gave, there's no question that it was nobler and more generous in the man who had received the offence to pardon it than to do otherwise. If the first miscarried for it, he's not to be blamed for his good intention; nor do we know whether, by acting otherwise, he'd have escaped the end his destiny had appointed him — and he'd at least have lost the glory of so humane an act.

You'll read in history of many who, fearing for their lives, took the course of meeting and pre-empting conspiracies by punishment and revenge; but I find very few who got any advantage from this — witness so many Roman emperors. Whoever finds himself in such danger ought not to expect much from his vigilance or his power. For how hard a thing it is to secure oneself from an enemy hiding behind the face of the most devoted friend, or to read the wills and inner thoughts of those in our personal service. It does little good to have a guard of foreigners around you and to be always fenced in by armed men: whoever despises his own life is master of yours. And besides, this continual suspicion, which makes a prince mistrustful of all the world, must of necessity be a strange torment to him. That's why Dion, when warned that Callippus was watching for an opportunity to take his life, never had the heart to inquire more closely into it. He said he'd rather die than live in that misery — having to stand continually on guard, not just against his enemies but against his friends too. Alexander demonstrated the same point even more vividly and more roundly in action when, having been warned by a letter from Parmenio that his most beloved physician Philip had been bought with Darius' money to poison him, he handed Philip the letter to read and at the same moment drank off the potion Philip had brought him. Wasn't this to express a resolution that if his friends meant to send him out of the world, he was willing to give them the opportunity? Alexander is the supreme model for daring acts; but I don't know whether there's another passage in his life that shows such firm courage as this, or so illustrious an image of the beauty and greatness of his mind.

Those who preach to princes such circumspect and vigilant jealousy and distrust in the name of security are preaching them ruin and dishonour. Nothing noble can be performed without danger. I know a man, naturally very daring and enterprising, whose good fortune is constantly spoiled by such persuasions — that he must keep himself closely surrounded by friends, must not listen to any reconciliation with old enemies, must hold himself aloof and never trust himself in hands stronger than his own, whatever promises or offers they may make, whatever advantages he may see in front of him. And I know another who has unexpectedly built his fortune by following the directly opposite advice.

Courage, whose reputation and glory men chase with such hungry appetite, presents itself when needed as magnificently in plain clothes as in full armour, in a private room as in a camp, with arms hanging down as with arms raised.

This over-cautious, over-wary prudence is a mortal enemy to all high and generous exploits. Scipio, in order to sound out Syphax's intentions, left his army, abandoned Spain — not yet secure or well settled in his new conquest — and crossed over into Africa in two small ships, to commit himself in an enemy country to the power of a barbarian king, on a faith untested and unknown, without any pledge, without hostages, on the sole security of the greatness of his own courage, his good fortune, and the promise of his high hopes.
"Habita fides ipsam plerumque fidem obligat."
["Trust often obliges fidelity." — Livy, xxii. 22.]

In a life of ambition and glory, you have to hold a tight rein on suspicion. Fear and distrust invite and draw on offence. The most mistrustful of our kings established his affairs chiefly by voluntarily putting his life and liberty into his enemies' hands — that act showing he had absolute confidence in them, so that they might place equal assurance in him. Caesar opposed only the authority of his face and the haughty sharpness of his rebukes to his mutinous legions in arms against him:
"Stetit aggere fulti Cespitis, intrepidus vultu: meruitque timeri, Nil metuens."
["He stood on a mound, his countenance intrepid, and earned the right to be feared, fearing nothing himself." — Lucan, v. 316.]

But it's also true that this undaunted assurance can't be represented in its full, pure form except by those whom the apprehension of death and the worst that can happen do not terrify. To go through the motions of a feigned resolution with a pale, doubtful face and trembling limbs, in service of some important reconciliation, will achieve nothing. It's an excellent way to win another's heart and goodwill, to submit and entrust oneself to him — provided it looks freely done, not forced by necessity, and in such a state that the man clearly does it out of complete confidence in the other party, or at least with a face untouched by any cloud of suspicion. When I was a boy I saw a gentleman, governor of a great city, who, faced with a popular uprising and fury and not knowing what else to do, walked out of a place of very great strength and safety to throw himself on the mercy of the seditious mob, hoping by that means to calm the tumult before it grew worse. It went badly for him: he was miserably killed there. Yet I don't think he committed so great a mistake in going out as people commonly reproach his memory with; his error was rather in choosing a gentle, submissive manner for his purpose, trying to quiet this storm by obeying rather than commanding, by entreaty rather than remonstrance. I'm inclined to think a gracious severity, with a soldierly way of issuing orders, full of confidence and authority appropriate to his rank and the dignity of his office, would have worked better for him — at any rate he'd have perished with more decency and reputation. There's nothing so impossible to expect from this many-headed monster in its fury as humanity and good nature; it is far more open to reverence and fear. I'd also reproach him that, having taken a resolution (brave rather than rash, in my judgment) to expose himself, weak and unprotected, on this tempestuous sea of raging madmen, he should have stuck to his role and not for an instant abandoned the lofty part he had undertaken. But once he saw the danger up close — and his nose happened to start bleeding — he switched the submissive, fawning expression he'd put on at first for one of fear and amazement, filled his voice with pleading and his eyes with tears, and tried to withdraw and save himself. That carriage only inflamed their fury, and soon brought its effects upon him.

On one occasion a general muster of several armed units was planned — and that's the most natural setting for secret reprisals, since they can be carried out there with greater safety. There were public and obvious signs that it wouldn't be safe for some of the officers whose duty it was to review them. A council was held, several plans proposed, as in a delicate and high-stakes matter. My own counsel, among the rest, was that they should at all costs avoid giving any sign of suspicion: the officers most at risk should ride boldly through the ranks with bright, confident faces, and instead of skimping on gunfire (as the majority were urging), they should ask the captains to order the soldiers to fire round, full volleys in honour of the spectators, sparing no powder. This was done, and served so well that it pleased the suspect troops and from then on bred mutual confidence and trust among them.

I look on Julius Caesar's way of winning men over as the best and finest you can practise. First he tried by clemency to make himself loved even by his enemies, contenting himself, when conspiracies were detected, with publicly announcing that he was already aware of them. After that, he made the noble resolution to wait without anxiety or fear for whatever might happen, surrendering himself entirely to the protection of the gods and of fortune — for, no question, that's the state he was in when he was killed.

A stranger, having publicly said he could teach Dionysius, the tyrant of Syracuse, an infallible method for uncovering all the conspiracies his subjects could contrive against him, if Dionysius would pay him a good sum for his trouble, was sent for. Dionysius wanted to learn so necessary an art. The man answered that the only art he knew was this: Dionysius should give him a talent of silver and then boast that he'd received an unparalleled secret from him. Dionysius liked the trick, and accordingly had six hundred crowns counted out to him. It wasn't likely he'd give so large a sum to an unknown man except on account of some extraordinary disclosure, and the belief in this kept his enemies on edge. Princes, in fact, are wise to publicise the information they receive about plots against their lives, so as to convince people they have such good intelligence that nothing can be plotted against them without their getting wind of it instantly. The Duke of Athens did many foolish things in setting up his new tyranny over Florence, but one stood out above the rest: receiving the first intimation of a conspiracy the people were hatching against him from Matteo di Morozzo, one of the conspirators, he promptly put Morozzo to death — to suppress the rumour, so that no one would think any of his subjects disliked his government.

I remember reading the story of some Roman of high rank who, fleeing the tyranny of the Triumvirate, had escaped a thousand times, by as many ingenious tricks, from falling into the hands of his pursuers. One day a troop of horse sent out to take him passed close by a thicket where he was crouching and very nearly missed spotting him. He considered, at that moment, the pains and difficulties he'd endured for so long evading the relentless searches made for him every day; the little pleasure he could hope for in such a life; and how much better it would be to die once for all than to live perpetually on this knife-edge. He rose up from his hiding place, called the soldiers back, showed them his form, and voluntarily delivered himself up to their cruelty — by that means freeing both himself and them from further trouble. To invite your enemies in to cut your throat seems an odd, extravagant resolution; and yet I think he did better to take that course than to live in continual feverish fear of an accident there was no cure for. Since all the remedies a man can apply to such a disease are full of restlessness and uncertainty, it's better, with manly courage, to brace oneself for the worst that can happen, and to take some comfort in knowing that the thing we fear may never come to pass.
